title: ⭐⭐ Revision: A Day at the Mall

questions.prompt: Where do you put a jacket on to see it on you, before you decide to buy it?
questions.explanation: The little room of the clothes shop where you try clothes on is the fitting room. The counter is where you pay, the mall is the whole building of shops, and the shop window is where the clothes are shown to the street.

questions.prompt: Your aunt wants a gold necklace for her birthday. Which shop sells it?
questions.explanation: Rings and necklaces, in gold or in silver, are the goods of the jewellery shop. The clothes shop sells blazers and sweaters, the toy shop sells toys, and the bakery sells bread and croissants.

questions.prompt: Complete with the past of the verb to shop: "We ___ in the mall all Sunday morning."
questions.explanation: Shop is a regular verb of one short syllable that ends in consonant, vowel, consonant, so its last letter doubles before the ending: shopped. The form shoped forgets the double letter, and shop and shops are present forms, which Sunday morning has already left behind.

questions.prompt: The T-shirt on the table costs only 5 dinars. Which word describes that price?
questions.explanation: Something that costs very little money is cheap, and 5 dinars for a T-shirt is very little. Expensive says the opposite, free would mean it costs nothing at all, and new speaks about the age of the T-shirt, not about its price.

questions.prompt: Complete: "I would like ___ the silver rings, please."
questions.explanation: When a verb follows would like, it always carries to in front of it: I would like to see the silver rings, please. The bare form see and the -ing form seeing never follow would like, and to seeing puts the two endings together, which English never allows.

questions.prompt: At the bakery, the customer gives the money and the shopkeeper gives the bread. Which sentence is true?

options.text: The shopkeeper pays for the bread.

questions.explanation: The one who gives the money buys, so the customer buys the bread and the shopkeeper sells it. The two sentences that make the shopkeeper buy or pay turn the shop upside down, and the customer who sells the bread does the shopkeeper's work.
